method: An iSCSI name is the SCSI device name of an iSCSI node, so it has to stay unique for the life of the node and must not encode an address. RFC 7143 defines three type designators. An iqn. name belongs to an authority that owns a domain: the page writes iqn., a date code yyyy-mm, a dot, the domain reversed label by label, and an optional colon-prefixed suffix. The date code is the first month in which that authority owned the domain, which is why one domain can carry different names over time; it is not the month the device was installed. DNS names are case-insensitive and an iSCSI name is compared as a normalized lower-case string, so the page lower-cases the domain and the suffix and drops one trailing dot, and it says so when it had to change what was typed. Each domain label holds 1 to 63 letters, digits or hyphens and cannot begin or end with a hyphen, and at least two labels are required because a single label is not a registered domain. The suffix is the authority's own string: letters, digits, dots, hyphens and colons, with no empty segment. The whole name is limited to 223 bytes, and the page starts warning at 200 characters. An eui. name carries exactly 16 hexadecimal digits and a naa. name an even number of hexadecimal digits up to 32, so both are checked for length and digits rather than assembled. The page checks the string form only: it does not test whether a name is unique in a fabric, whether the domain is still owned, or whether a given initiator or target will accept it, and the role, initiator or target, comes from the login and not from the name. Everything runs in the browser with no network access or storage.
